mcqs.q: Cell injury is defined as:
opts: The functional and morphological effects of stresses on a cell
A type of cell adaptation only
mcqs.explain: Cell injury is the functional and morphological effects of various stresses (etiologic agents) that change the cell's internal/external environment.

mcqs.q: The MAIN cause of cell injury is:
mcqs.explain: Hypoxia (decreased oxygen supply) is the main cause of cell injury.

mcqs.q: Which is a cause of HYPOXIA?
mcqs.explain: Hypoxia results from ischaemia (arterial occlusion/atherosclerosis), inadequate oxygenation (lung disease) or reduced O₂-carrying capacity (anaemia).

mcqs.q: Ischaemia refers to:
mcqs.explain: Ischaemia is reduced blood supply, e.g. from arterial occlusion or atherosclerosis — a common cause of hypoxic injury.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a recognised cause of cell injury?
mcqs.explain: Causes include hypoxia, infectious/physical/chemical agents, immunological reactions, nutritional and genetic disorders — adequate oxygenation is normal, not injurious.

mcqs.q: Which is a MECHANISM of cell injury?
opts: ATP depletion and increased intracellular calcium
mcqs.explain: Mechanisms include ATP depletion, increased membrane permeability, calcium entry (activating enzymes), mitochondrial damage and free-radical formation.

mcqs.q: Increased intracellular calcium injures the cell by:
mcqs.explain: Calcium entering the cell activates destructive cellular enzymes (proteases, phospholipases, etc.).

mcqs.q: Whether cell injury is reversible or irreversible depends mainly on the:
opts: Severity and duration of the injurious agent
mcqs.explain: The outcome depends on the severity and duration of the injurious agent: mild/brief = reversible; severe/prolonged = irreversible (death).

mcqs.q: The three forms of REVERSIBLE cell injury are:
opts: Cloudy swelling, hydropic swelling and fatty change
mcqs.explain: Reversible cell injury has three forms: cloudy swelling, hydropic swelling and fatty change; necrosis/apoptosis are irreversible.

mcqs.q: Cloudy swelling is characterised microscopically by:
opts: Swollen cells with fine-granular cytoplasm and a normal nucleus
mcqs.explain: Cloudy swelling shows swollen cells with red fine-granular cytoplasm (water accumulation) and a normal nucleus.

mcqs.q: The pathogenesis of cloudy swelling involves:
opts: ATP depletion → Na-K pump failure → sodium and water entry
mcqs.explain: Hypoxia reduces ATP, so the Na-K pump fails; sodium accumulates and water enters the cell, causing swelling (worsened by lactic-acid build-up).

mcqs.q: On gross examination, an organ with cloudy swelling is:
mcqs.explain: The affected organ is enlarged and swollen, pale (compressed capillaries), soft and heavy.

mcqs.q: In both cloudy and hydropic swelling, the nucleus is:
mcqs.explain: In reversible swelling injury the nucleus remains normal; nuclear changes (pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis) indicate irreversible injury/necrosis.

mcqs.q: Hydropic swelling differs from cloudy swelling by showing:
opts: Cytoplasmic vacuoles from excess water (a more advanced lesion)
mcqs.explain: Hydropic swelling is a more advanced reversible lesion with multiple cytoplasmic vacuoles from excess water; the nucleus is still normal.

mcqs.q: Fatty change is the pathological accumulation of:
mcqs.explain: Fatty change is accumulation of excess neutral fat because injured cells cannot metabolise fat (reduced enzyme activity).

mcqs.q: Fatty change occurs most commonly in the ___ because it is the major organ of fat metabolism:
mcqs.explain: The liver is the commonest site of fatty change as it is the major organ of fat metabolism (also heart, muscle, kidney).

mcqs.q: Which is a cause of fatty change?
opts: Alcohol, obesity, diabetes, protein malnutrition or toxins
mcqs.explain: Fatty change follows alcohol, obesity, protein malnutrition, diabetes mellitus and toxins.

mcqs.q: Irreversible cell injury results in cell death by:
mcqs.explain: Irreversible injury (severe/prolonged) leads to cell death by necrosis or apoptosis.

mcqs.q: Anaemia causes hypoxic cell injury by:
opts: Reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
mcqs.explain: Anaemia reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, producing hypoxia even with normal blood flow and ventilation.

mcqs.q: Free-radical formation injures cells primarily by:
mcqs.explain: Free radicals are highly reactive and damage cell membranes, proteins and DNA — one of the key mechanisms of cell injury.

mcqs.q: If the injurious stimulus is removed during cloudy swelling, the cell will:
mcqs.explain: Cloudy swelling is reversible; if injury stops the cell returns to normal, but if it continues it progresses to hydropic swelling and beyond.

mcqs.q: ATP depletion in cell injury is a direct consequence of:
opts: Inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation by damaged mitochondria
mcqs.explain: Hypoxia/mitochondrial damage inhibits oxidative phosphorylation, depleting ATP — the central event triggering pump failure and swelling.

saqs.q: Define cell injury and name its main cause.
saqs.a: The functional and morphological effects of stresses on a cell. Main cause: hypoxia (ischaemia, lung disease, anaemia).

saqs.q: List the mechanisms of cell injury.
saqs.a: ATP depletion, increased membrane permeability, calcium entry (enzyme activation), mitochondrial damage, free-radical formation.

saqs.q: Name the three forms of reversible cell injury.
saqs.a: Cloudy swelling, hydropic swelling, and fatty change.

saqs.q: Explain the pathogenesis of cloudy swelling.
saqs.a: Hypoxia → ↓ ATP → Na-K pump failure → sodium and water enter the cell; anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acid → ↑ osmotic pressure → more water entry → swelling.

saqs.q: Give the gross and microscopic features of cloudy swelling.
saqs.a: Gross: enlarged, pale, soft, heavy organ. Micro: swollen cells, fine-granular cytoplasm, normal nucleus.
Cloudy: granular cytoplasm (water). Hydropic: cytoplasmic vacuoles (excess water) — a more advanced lesion. Both have a normal nucleus.

saqs.q: Define fatty change and list its causes.
saqs.a: Accumulation of excess neutral fat (injured cells can't metabolise fat), commonest in the liver. Causes: alcohol, obesity, diabetes, protein malnutrition, toxins.
